title: Why averaging many trees improves regression

items.stem: A forest averages 200 deep regression trees, each trained on a different bootstrap sample. Compared with one deep tree, what does the averaging mainly change?

options.text: It lowers the variance and leaves the bias about the same
It lowers the bias and leaves the variance about the same
It lowers both the bias and the variance by a lot
It raises the bias and leaves the variance about the same

items.stem: Each tree in a forest has prediction variance 9 at some input, and any two trees have correlation 0.25. What is the variance of the average of 3 such trees? Use Var = rho*sigma^2 + (1 - rho)*sigma^2/B.
A random forest lets each split consider only a random subset of the features. Why does that help the averaged prediction?

options.text: Each tree then fits the training rows exactly, with no error
The trees become less alike, which lowers the variance floor
Each tree then needs fewer rows, so training is more accurate
The trees become more alike, which lowers the variance floor

items.stem: A forest is trained on houses of 1,000 to 3,000 square feet, with prices rising steadily with size. In one sentence, what will it predict for a 5,000-square-foot house, and why?
Trees in a forest have correlation 0.4 with each other. You grow the forest from 500 trees to 5,000 trees. What happens to the variance of the average?

options.text: It falls by about a factor of ten
It rises, because the forest now overfits more
It barely changes, as it is near its floor
It falls to nearly zero as trees are added
